name: Darcy's law
seoDesc: Darcy's law: work out flow rate (Q) from the pressure difference and the viscosity. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: flow rate (Q) is what the Darcy's law calculator works out, and it gets there from the pressure difference, the viscosity, the distance and the area. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Darcy's law calculator work?
sections.html:
The Darcy's law calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports flow rate (Q) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the pressure difference (Δp), the viscosity (μ), the distance (L) and the area (A).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Darcy's law calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Flow rate (Q)=area (A) × hydraulic gradient (I) × permeability (k)
Pressure out=-pressure difference (Δp) + pressure in
Hydraulic gradient (I)=pressure difference (Δp) ÷ (distance (L) × viscosity (μ))
Volume (V)=area (A) × hydraulic gradient (I) × permeability (k) × time (t)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Viscosity – dynamic, opening in pascal seconds
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Darcy's law calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the pressure difference, the viscosity and the distance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Darcy's law calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns flow rate (Q), derived from the pressure difference, the viscosity and the distance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Darcy's law calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the pressure difference, the viscosity, the distance and the area, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter pressure in in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Pressure in opens in pascals and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Darcy's law calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
